newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Record fine for Deutsche UK fund arm.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Record fine for Deutsche UK fund arm.

text.p: Investment watchdog IMRO on Wednesday fined Deutsche Bank's British fund arm a record two million pounds ($3.3 million) for a catalogue of rule breaches and management failings.

The Investment Management Regulatory Organisation also imposed costs of a million pounds on two Morgan Grenfell Asset Management (MGAM) subsidiaries and lambasted them for not informing it of concerns about fund managers.
It said at least one MGAM board member had been told of problems at the funds, two of which were managed by Peter Young, by April 1996.
Difficulties at three MGAM funds emerged last September when they were temporarily suspended due to serious irregularities in the valuation of unlisted securities.

German parent Deutsche Bank made a cash injection of 180 million pounds into the funds and Young was suspended and later dismissed. Deutsche reached a swift compensation agreement with IMRO last December and is expected to pay out around 220 million pounds to investors, a factor taken into account by IMRO in its fine.

IMRO said it had yet to reach its conclusions about the individuals responsible for the management and supervision of the Morgan Grenfell European Growth Trust, the Morgan Grenfell Europa Fund and the Dublin-based Morgan Grenfell European Capital Growth Fund.
Two of these were managed by Young whose activities are being probed by the Serious Fraud Office. Young has denied any criminal activity.
IMRO chief executive Phillip Thorpe said the mismanagement had "caused unnecessary concern to an enormous number of investors". Around 90,000 retail investors had money invested in funds.
"The management of Morgan Grenfell failed to control the operation of its business and ignored clear and repeated warnings with severe adverse financial results," Thorpe added.
In a detailed statement, IMRO said the irregularities were connected with, but not limited to, Young's activities.

It said Morgan Grenfell International Funds Management had not ensured that the managers of the funds were adequately supervised despite concerns about the inappropriate use of investment companies to circumvent regulations, the unusually high proportion of unlisted securities and their repeated failure to provide evidence of due diligence.
IMRO also said there had been repeated attempts by the fund managers "to exploit perceived loopholes in the regulations" as well as other activities that ought to have set alarm bells ringing.

MGAM chief executive Robert Smith, who replaced previous head Keith Percy in the aftermath of the affair, said that failings in the unit trust business had been addressed and that compliance, controls and operating methods had been subjected to rigorous review.
Percy, along with directors Glyn Owen, Graham Kane and Michael Wheatley all left the firm in October after an internal probe into the irregularities found management failings.

Smith told Reuters that important changes had been made, including imposing a list of known companies which fund managers were allowed to invest in and a rigorous vetting procedure if they wanted to stray from this list.

Other changes included MGAM's compliance head now reporting directly to Deutsche Morgan Grenfell and in turn to Deutsche Bank, and MGAM's deal management system being altered to ring alarm bells if large percentages of funds were invested in one company.

"I think we are now one of the best regulated firms in the City of London," Smith said, adding he was proud of MGAM's superior investment performance. "We have not lost people and we have not lost clients. There has been a net asset business gain since," he added.
He conceded that the growth in funds under management before the problems had been far greater than the rise since, although he expects this to build again through the summer period.
Smith said the firm had acted in an exemplary way in dealing with the fallout and morale was good. "I'd like to feel this is us now drawing a line under the affair," he added.
Banking analYsts said the long-term effect on Deutsche's global investment banking ambitions was impossible to establish.
"Its not really possible to quantify the impact on the future growth of the business," said one, noting that Deutsche had already accounted for the compensation payments in its 1996 earnings.
